title: Specification of the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Protocol for the Exchange of Flow Information
summary: This document specifies the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) protocol, which transmits traffic flow information over the network. It describes how Data and Template Records are carried over several transport protocols from an Exporting Process to a Collecting Process. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: IPFIX sends records about observed network traffic from an exporter to a collector. Templates describe each record's fields so collectors can interpret data from different exporters.

questions: how to export network flow data
how does ipfix differ from netflow
subtitle: A standard message format for exporting measured network-flow records to collectors.

tldr.problem: Network elements measure traffic flows, but a collector needs a common format to receive records from many exporters and understand their fields.
tldr.mechanism: An Exporting Process sends IPFIX messages containing templates and data sets to a Collecting Process. SCTP is required; TCP and UDP are optional transports.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7011 is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 5101 and remains interoperable with it. It specifies transport security support and how sequence numbers expose record loss.

today: RFC 7011 is an Internet Standard (STD 77) and obsoletes RFC 5101. Its IPFIX protocol remains interoperable with that earlier specification.

sections.title: Flows, Exporters and Collectors
sections.content:
A flow is a set of packets or frames that share properties and pass an observation point during a time interval. Its defining properties, called flow keys, can come from packet headers, packet characteristics, or how the network treated packets.

A metering process creates flow records. An exporting process sends those records to one or more collecting processes in IPFIX messages. This RFC defines the message format, templates, transports, and security considerations; the names and meanings of information elements are defined separately.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow groups packets that share selected properties, such as addresses and ports. An exporter sends records about those flows to a collector.

sections.title: The Message Header and Sets
sections.content:
An IPFIX message starts with a header and contains zero or more Sets. A Set contains records of one type: data records, template records, or options template records. The four-octet Set header identifies the Set type and gives its length, including any padding.

The message header carries the version, total length, export time, sequence number, and observation domain identifier. Version 0x000a identifies the version specified here. The sequence number counts data records modulo 2^32, letting a collector detect missing records; template records do not advance it.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message has a header followed by sets of records. Header fields identify the version, size, time, record counter, and observation domain.

sections.title: Templates Define Record Layouts
sections.content:
A Template Record lists, in order, the fields that appear in each matching Data Record. Each field specification identifies an information element and its length. The Data Set uses the Template ID as its Set ID, so a collector needs the matching template to interpret the field values.

Template IDs range from 256 to 65535 and are unique within a transport session and observation domain. An Options Template adds scope fields that specify which records its other fields describe. Exporters may also define enterprise-specific information elements by including an enterprise number.
sections.plainLanguage: A template describes the fields and their order. The data records that use it contain values, and the collector needs that template to read them.

sections.title: Field Encoding, Time and Variable Lengths
sections.content:
Most IPFIX values use network byte order. Strings use UTF-8, while octet arrays are raw bytes. Reduced-size encoding lets an exporter use fewer bytes for some integers or floating-point values when the value fits; the template records the chosen field length.

A variable-length field is marked with length 65535 in its template. Each value then carries its length before the data: one octet for lengths below 255, or three octets when the value is longer. Some timestamps use 32-bit seconds since the UNIX epoch and can wrap; exporters and collectors use modulo arithmetic and contextual time to interpret them.
sections.plainLanguage: The template records how long each field is, and some fields can carry their own length. Exporters and collectors must also account for timestamp counters that wrap around.

sections.title: Keeping Templates in Sync
sections.content:
The exporter assigns template IDs for each transport session and observation domain. It should send a template before sending data that uses it, but a collector must not assume the template and data arrive in the same message. A template applies only during its defined lifetime and cannot be reused from an earlier transport session.

For reliable transports, an exporter can withdraw a template by sending a template record with a field count of zero. UDP cannot reliably deliver templates, so exporters must retransmit active templates periodically and must not send withdrawals. Over UDP, a collector replaces a template when a different definition arrives for an already-used ID.
sections.plainLanguage: The exporter sends templates so the collector can read later data. Because UDP can lose messages, exporters using it repeat templates and do not send withdrawals.

sections.title: SCTP, TCP and UDP Transport
sections.content:
Every compliant implementation must support SCTP with its partial-reliability extension. TCP and UDP are optional. SCTP provides congestion control and can choose the reliability used for data; TCP is reliable but may block an exporter when congestion persists. UDP has no congestion control or delivery guarantee and is permitted only when the application can tolerate message loss.

The default collector ports are 4739 for ordinary transport and 4740 for secure transport. A message can be up to 65535 octets. If a UDP path's maximum transmission unit is unknown, the RFC recommends a maximum packet size of 512 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: SCTP is required and supports controlled delivery choices. TCP delivers reliably but can stall; UDP can lose messages and needs a path that can handle the traffic.

sections.title: Protecting Flow Data and Collectors
sections.content:
Flow records can reveal network configuration and user traffic. IPFIX requires mechanisms for confidentiality, integrity, and authentication between exporters and collectors. The RFC requires implementations to support TLS for TCP and DTLS for SCTP or UDP, and requires mutual authentication when these security protocols are used.

Collectors must check message, Set, and variable-field lengths for consistency and discard malformed messages. They should track sequence numbers to detect insertion or loss. The collected data may be personally identifiable, so the collector must protect its storage through technical and policy measures.
sections.plainLanguage: Flow records may contain sensitive information, so exporters and collectors need authenticated, protected communication. Collectors must validate lengths and protect the records they store.
